title: Writing from a parallel job
sub: ParallelWriter with capacity up front, the queue, the hash map and NativeStream, two passes with a prefix sum
cards/0/body:
In an IJobParallelFor the iterations run on different threads at the same time. That is why the safety system in the Editor lets Execute(i) write to a NativeArray only at its own index i; writing to another index throws. The [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction] attribute lifts that ban, but then guaranteeing there are no races is on you.

Often you do not know the size of the result in advance: out of 10,000 objects, say, 700 are visible. You cannot pack them densely “at your own index”, and a plain NativeList.Add from several threads is a race: two threads take the same slot, and growing the list reallocates the buffer while others are writing into it. Unity will not even schedule such a job: in the Editor Schedule() throws — the container does not support parallel writing.
cards/1/body:
Lists, queues and hash maps have a nested ParallelWriter type, which you get from AsParallelWriter(). The NativeList<T> writer can do one thing — AddNoResize: atomically take the next slot and write into it. It cannot grow: there is no safe way to reallocate a buffer while other threads are writing into it.

Hence the rule: capacity up front, at the upper bound. For a filter that is the input length. Overflowing it in the Editor throws InvalidOperationException; a regular build has no such checks, and the write goes past the end of the buffer.

And the second rule: the order is nondeterministic. Indices land in whatever order the threads got there, and it differs from run to run.
cards/2/q: Why does the list’s ParallelWriter have AddNoResize but no Add?
cards/2/options/0: Growing means reallocating the buffer, and that cannot be done safely while other threads write into the same buffer
cards/2/options/1: Add is slower, so it was removed for the sake of speed under Burst
cards/2/options/2: Add exists, it just does not compile under Burst
cards/2/options/3: In a parallel job the list length is fixed, so you cannot add at all
cards/2/explain: The writer only takes the next slot with an atomic counter. Memory cannot be reallocated while other threads write into it without a lock, so you set the capacity up front — at the upper bound of the result.
cards/2/wrong/1: It is not about speed: there is simply no safe way to grow from several threads.
cards/2/wrong/2: The list’s ParallelWriter has no Add method at all; Burst has nothing to do with it.
cards/2/wrong/3: The length does grow — every AddNoResize increments it by 1. Only the capacity does not grow.
cards/3/task: Finish the visibility filter. In CullJob add a field visible of type NativeList<int>.ParallelWriter and in Execute append the index to it with AddNoResize. In ScheduleCull create the list with capacity positions.Length (Allocator.TempJob), give the job its AsParallelWriter() and schedule the job over positions.Length (second argument 64).
cards/3/checks/1/label: The index is appended with AddNoResize
cards/3/checks/3/label: The list is created with a capacity and Allocator.TempJob
cards/3/checks/5/label: The job is scheduled over positions.Length
cards/3/explain: Capacity positions.Length is the upper bound: there cannot be more visible items than items. AddNoResize takes a slot atomically, so the threads do not get in each other’s way. The order of indices in visible changes from run to run — if it matters, sort afterwards or collect differently.
cards/4/body:
NativeQueue<T> is a queue built from a chain of blocks. Its constructor takes no capacity: the AsParallelWriter() writer with its Enqueue(x) adds blocks by itself, so you do not have to work out the size in advance. You read it later on one thread with TryDequeue or ToArray. As with the list, the order across threads is not guaranteed.

NativeParallelHashMap<K,V> is a hash map with ParallelWriter.TryAdd(key, value), which returns false if the key is already there. You set the capacity up front — the parallel writer will not grow it. For several values per key there is NativeParallelMultiHashMap, the classic spatial hash: cell → indices of the objects in it.

A Collections 2.x trap: NativeHashMap is single-threaded and has no AsParallelWriter(). In Collections 2.1 the old map was renamed to NativeParallelHashMap, and the name NativeHashMap went to a new one — without parallel writing.
cards/5/title: NativeStream: a buffer per index and a stable order
cards/5/body:
NativeStream is a set of independent append-only buffers. You set the number of buffers when you create it; each buffer is written by one writer and read by one reader, with no synchronisation. A buffer grows in blocks without copying, so no capacity is needed up front.

In a parallel job you usually keep one buffer per iteration (or per batch of iterations): BeginForEachIndex(i), any number of Write calls, EndForEachIndex(). The reader then walks the buffers by index — and the result comes out in the same order on every run, however the threads were distributed. The price is one more step: read the stream and lay the result out (often the next job does it).
cards/6/title: Two passes: count → prefix sum → write
cards/6/body:
A technique from parallel algorithms that maps neatly onto jobs. When each element produces an unknown number of results and you need a dense array with a stable order:

  1. Count. A parallel job writes counts[i] — how many results element i will produce. That is a write at its own index, so the safety system’s restriction holds.
  2. Prefix sum. An IJob walks counts and writes offsets[i] — the sum of everything before it (an exclusive scan), and puts the grand total into a NativeReference.
  3. Write. A parallel job writes element i’s results into output starting at offsets[i]. The ranges do not overlap, but this is not “its own index”, so output needs [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction].

No atomics, a deterministic order, one dense array as the result. The price is two passes over the data and a scan on one thread; you allocate output at the upper bound.
cards/7/q: Put the steps of the two-pass write in order.
cards/7/items/0: CountJob: each element writes counts[i] at its own index
cards/7/items/1: ScanJob: offsets[i] is the sum of counts before i, total is the sum of all
cards/7/items/2: WriteJob: element i writes its results into output starting at offsets[i]
cards/7/items/3: Complete() the last job and read output from 0 to total
cards/7/explain: Each step depends on the previous one, so the three jobs form a chain through dependsOn, and Complete() is called once, at the end. The prefix sum turns “how many” into “where”, and the second parallel pass writes with no atomics and no races.
cards/8/q: Match the task with a way to collect results from a parallel job
cards/8/pairs/0/0: Filter indices, the upper bound is known
cards/8/pairs/1/0: Events with no upper bound, order does not matter
cards/8/pairs/3/0: The same order on every run
cards/8/pairs/3/1: NativeStream or two passes with a prefix sum
cards/9/q: What is true about writing from a parallel job? Select all.
cards/9/options/0: If the capacity runs out, AddNoResize throws in the Editor
cards/9/options/2: NativeQueue.ParallelWriter does not need a preset capacity
cards/9/options/3: The order of elements after AddNoResize is the same on every run
cards/9/options/4: In the second pass of the prefix-sum scheme, output needs [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction]
cards/9/explain: Overflowing AddNoResize in the Editor throws InvalidOperationException; a build has no check. NativeHashMap in 2.x is single-threaded; for parallel writing use NativeParallelHashMap. The queue grows in blocks by itself. The ParallelWriter order depends on which thread got there first. In the second pass element i writes not at its own index but into its own range, so the restriction is lifted with the attribute.
cards/10/q: Interviewer: “You need a list of contacts from a parallel job, and in a replay it must match bit for bit. How do you collect it?”
cards/10/options/0: NativeStream with a buffer per index, or two passes with a prefix sum: the element’s index decides the order, not whichever thread got there first
cards/10/options/1: NativeList.ParallelWriter: AddNoResize is atomic, so the order is stable too
cards/10/options/2: NativeQueue.ParallelWriter: a queue keeps the order of insertion
cards/10/options/3: Any ParallelWriter: under Burst the threads always run in the same order
cards/10/explain: Atomicity protects against a race; it does not set the order. A stable order comes from schemes where the index determines where a result goes: NativeStream (read the buffers in order) or count → prefix sum → write. Another option is ParallelWriter plus a sort afterwards, but that is an extra O(n log n) pass.
cards/10/wrong/1: The atomic counter guarantees that slots never collide, but who takes a slot first is up to the scheduler.
cards/10/wrong/2: The queue hands elements out in insertion order, but with parallel writers that order itself depends on the threads and is not guaranteed.
cards/10/wrong/3: Burst has no effect on how the scheduler hands iterations to threads.
